title: A private ranch that wants 2,000 acres of federal land in Colorado has spent $200,000 to lobby a congressman
text:
Stated Claim / Post Context:
A private ranch that wants 2,000 acres of federal land in Colorado has spent $200,000 to lobby a congressman

A wealthy ranch owner’s land exchange proposal would privatize thousands of acres of public land in the Roaring Fork Valley. It has rankled locals, who say the deal would sidestep normal processes.

A wealthy ranch owner’s land exchange proposal — which would privatize thousands of acres of public land in Colorado’s Roaring Fork Valley — has rankled locals, who say they have been left in the dark and that the deal would sidestep normal regulatory processes.

Under the proposal, Out of Bounds Ranch would swap approximately 2,100 acres of private land north of Rifle for a similarly-sized parcel of federal public land adjacent to the ranch property near Carbondale. The ranch’s owners have worked with a Western Slope congressman to draft a bill authorizing the land swap instead of pursuing the Bureau of Land Management administrative process for such exchanges.

The ranch’s out-of-state owners have spent six figures on federal lobbying and donated to U.S. Rep. Jeff Hurd’s campaign, records show, as they’ve sought congressional action on the matter.

They say the swap would improve their ranch operations and also make federal land near Rifle more accessible to the public.

But those who use the land the ranch seeks don’t want to lose access and are dismayed by what they see as an unfair process.

“One of my biggest concerns is that it deletes over 2,000 acres of public land around the Glenwood Springs area,” said Tayler Larsen, whose family has hunted on the BLM parcel for more than 30 years. “And it’s gone forever.”

B. Scott Smith and Tiffany Smith bought their 1,900-acre property near Carbondale for $8.5 million in 2021 and named it Out of Bounds Ranch. Scott Smith, a co-founder of an expansive car dealership company and another company that owns 11 racing speedways, operates it as a working cattle ranch. He says he and his wife plan to permanently move from their home in North Carolina to the ranch property in the future.

The land exchange would more than double the size of their ranch. The swap is necessary, Smith said, for more coherent management of grazing, fencing and the land as a whole. The ranch already grazes its cattle on the adjacent public parcel through a lease with the BLM.

On the other side of the exchange, the transfer of now-private property would connect two large parcels of BLM land outside of Rifle, making it a contiguous area of public land — one of the ranch’s primary selling points for the swap.

“The goal is a genuine win-win-win: better management for the ranch, substantially improved public access and recreation, and meaningful conservation and wildlife benefits,” Smith wrote in an email in response to questions from The Denver Post.

The Smiths first approached the BLM in October 2021 about a potential land exchange, according to the ranch. They contacted the agency again in April 2025 and spoke with the state director at the time, who said the process could take more than a decade and would not be a priority for his limited staff.

BLM staff also said they hesitated to pursue administrative land exchanges because those often prompt litigation, Smith said.

“Based on meetings, site visits, telephone conversations, and that history, it became apparent that BLM did not have a predictable administrative path, the available personnel, or the institutional willingness to initiate and complete an administrative exchange of this complexity within a reasonable period,” Smith told The Post.

Federal law prescribes a method for public land to be exchanged for private land through an internal process at the BLM. But Congress can also authorize an exchange, with fewer mandatory steps involved — a route the Smiths soon began to explore.

The ranch in June 2025 pivoted to discussions with Hurd, the Republican representing Colorado’s 3rd Congressional District, about a legislative approach to the exchange.

At the same time, the Smiths began pouring money into lobbying.

Between April 2025 and June 2026, the ranch paid $200,000 to lobbying firms to advocate for the land exchange
